item.title: Custom Solutions Upgrade and Easier Preflop ICM Setup
item.description: Custom solutions now go 1,000bb deep, GTO Wizard AI can choose your 3-way bet sizes, and you can load any tournament spot directly from a hand history.
item.dc:creator: GTO Wizard
item.content:encoded:
Hello Wizards,

Today we're releasing a set of improvements to custom solutions:

  • Solve up to 1,000bb deep (previously 250bb)
  • Postflop SPR up to 500 (previously 125)
  • Retrained Hold'em models: GTO Wizard AI is now even more accurate across all spots
  • Automatic & Dynamic sizing for all 3-way postflop spots
  • Preflop ICM solving straight from your hand history or tournament JSON
  • Mystery bounty solving is now available

Solve up to 1,000bb deep, with SPR up to 500

  • Stack depth: up to 1,000bb, previously 250bb.
  • Postflop SPR: up to 500, previously 125.

Built for deep cash games and for spots where the effective stack is many times the pot, like limped pots.

GTO Wizard AI, now even more accurate

We retrained every Hold'em model, including preflop ICM. The result: even more precise solutions, in every situation and on every street.

To illustrate the improvement, we picked our 3-way turn benchmark. Average EV loss dropped 16.8% versus the July 2025 release, from 0.2415% to 0.2009% of the pot. The worst turn improved from 0.5954% to 0.4401%.

Automatic & Dynamic sizing for 3-way postflop spots

When 3-way solving launched, you had to choose every bet size by hand. Today we're adding a feature you've been asking for: automatic and dynamic sizing. GTO Wizard AI picks the highest-EV sizes for you in any 3-way spot, and it works with both cEV and ICM models.

Preflop ICM solving straight from your hand history

Upload a hand history or a tournament JSON and solve any tournament spot in a couple of seconds. Payouts, stacks, players left and average stack all fill in for you.

  • Upload a hand history: GTO Wizard reads the tournament ID, loads the matching payouts and fills in every player's stack. Hands already in the Analyzer open the same way with one click on Study.
  • Players left and average stack: estimated for you.
  • PKO and KO bounties: read from the hand history.
  • Preset Library: tournaments from PokerStars, WPN, Winamax, 888poker and more. Filter by format, buy-in, field size, prize pool and seats, or search by name or tournament ID.
  • No exact match? You get a similar tournament instead.
  • Final table deals: flagged when a deal changed the payouts.
  • JSON import: for any other site. It stays private to your account and saves as a preset for next time.
  • Redesigned Custom Solutions modal: a cleaner flow from upload to solve.

Coming next: solve any spot straight from a screenshot 👀

Mystery bounty, solved in 3 steps

We made solving mystery bounty much easier. Here's all it takes:

  1. Pick Mystery bounty in hand details.
  2. Enter the payouts (GTO Wizard AI calculates the initial bounty prize pool for you, or estimates it when the exact figure isn't available).
  3. Add the average bounty (or let GTO Wizard AI calculate it from players left and bounties left) and solve.

Try it now

See the custom solutions upgrade in action. Run a 1,000bb cash spot, or upload your hand history and solve any tournament spot you faced in a couple of seconds.

item.title: How to Exploit Capped Ranges with Custom Aggregated Reports
item.description:
Have you ever considered how capping your range preflop would shift your postflop strategy?
In this article, Barry Carter uses Custom Aggregated Reports to analyze the global cost of capping your preflop range by excluding specific hand classes from your raising range.
item.dc:creator: Barry Carter
item.content:encoded:
The custom aggregated reports are my new favorite feature. I already loved the (presolved) flop reports tool, but these custom ones let you zoom out and view the general approach to optimal strategy when facing imperfect players and ranges. ɑ

Today, I wanted to look at the global strategic changes postflop we should make when our opponent has capped their preflop range in tournaments. This is something I often see in the games I play. Quite simply, the ranges are too tight and do not include board coverage, especially 3-betting ranges. 

There are player populations where, when 3-betting, they always have a very strong hand, and very little in the way of bluffs. How should we play against these players?

As is always the case in my articles, a reminder that I am not a professional player, I am a writer who knows his way around solvers and is using them to fix his leaks. Not only do the players in my games have the leak we are going to explore, but I am guilty of it myself from time to time. 

Ranges Without Board Coverage

Before looking at 3-betting ranges, let’s first tackle the question of how to proceed against players whose ranges are not well-rounded enough to cover all possible boards sufficiently. This is something I explored in my article on board coverage; however, I cherry-picked the hands at the time. Now I can look at what happens on every single strategically distinct flop. 

In short, board coverage refers to ensuring that a range includes all potentially strong hands on any given flop. For example, below are the GTO ranges for a single-raised pot between UTG and BB with 100bb stacks:

UTG has a tight range, but it includes a lot of suited Ace-x and King-x. The Ace-x goes down to A3s. While the old-school wisdom would argue that these are ‘dominated’ hands, what they offer is a very economical way to hit a lot of different flops. We always potentially have flush draws and flushes, we can make low straights, and we have the potential to make trips on low-paired boards.  

Let’s compare this to a range where that is less the case. We kept the BB range the same, but the UTG range is now much more high-card-heavy, while still representing a similar percentage of overall hands. They do have all the pocket pairs in this range, so they are more likely to make sets, but if a low-paired board came, the only time their hand could contain that low card is when they made quads. 

For the same reason, low straights are very hard to make for them. When it comes to flushes, suited cards are now a smaller proportion of their range, thereby also lowering the likelihood of making flushes. What we have done is ‘capped’ the UTG range, making certain nutted hands much less likely. 

In my board coverage article, I picked low flops that these players would obviously struggle with. This time, I have run two custom aggregated reports—one with the GTO ranges and the other with the capped UTG range—to see what the global adjustments are.

Note: The BB can gain EV against this new UTG range by deviating from their GTO strategy; their calling range would likely get tighter because UTG is more weighted towards pairs and strong Ace-x. However, we maintained the BB’s strategy because we’re interested in the effects of a capped range on postflop strategy. If we compared the reports, one in which both ranges were modified, we wouldn’t know to what extent the capped preflop range caused the change in strategy. 

Comparing Performance Metrics

Before analyzing the strategic changes, the first data points I like to look at in these reports are the three major performance metrics: expected value (EV), equity (EQ), and equity realization (EQR). They give an overall impression of who is performing better across the 1755 flops.  

These are from the root node; the metrics change in response to each action taken by a player. However, I think that the first node, before any postflop actions have been taken, is the most telling of the cost of capping your range.

The equities differ slightly because the ranges are different. The equity realization also differs; we will cover that later in this article.

The difference in EV is most interesting for now; 0.07bb might not sound much, but as I often like to frame it, that would be a 70 bb/100 error over a large sample. A cash game player would wince when they see that. 

So, without even peeking at the strategic changes, we can see that capping our range in a way that reduces board coverage is costly. Now let’s look at how it might cost us. 

BB’s First Action

Going from ~99% checking overall to ~96% is a small difference in the big picture. However, in relative terms, that means there’s four times more leading than at equilibrium. Also, notice the BB’s preference is now going toward the smaller lead size.

This should make sense; the boards with more leads will be low and connected (e.g., 654r). The increase in leading is an example of attacking a capped range. If UTG were smart, they would recognize they can’t raise very often in these spots and should also check back on these boards a lot. So the BB leads to exploit the capped range and to get thin value. 

When the BB Checks

The change in frequency compared to the previous node is pretty similar here; from checking back ~19% of the time to ~21%. The more significant shift in strategy relates to the bet sizes. You’ll notice that the bet sizes get larger as a result. A much more polarized strategy is adopted because, with some hands missing from the range, they find themselves having either a strong hand or a complete miss more often. In addition, the larger bet sizings might also be because their range benefits more from protection. When you have strong hands like overpairs and top pair, but it’s much harder for you to have low straights and flushes, you are incentivized to bet big to price out draws. 

Caveat: In reality, the player with the capped range might not understand they have a capped range, and will still c-bet most of the time for a smaller amount. What we are seeing here is the strategy the solver identified as ‘best possible’ for the capped range we forced upon it. 

When UTG Bets 67% Pot

The most common c-bet size between the two examples is 67% pot, so let’s look at the response to it.

The BB folds more often in capped world, because UTG has a stronger preflop range. The BB also raises more; 11.5% of the time compared to 10.4% of the time. They favor the smaller raise size, which is more than enough to put pressure on a capped range.

Not taking care of board coverage costs EV. Such ranges can be exploited by being tighter and more aggressive. So fold more, but when you play, consider leading and check-raising more often.

When Villain Has No Bluffs

Now, let’s look at the situation I described at the start of this article, which is players who never have bluffs in their preflop 3-betting range. I really wanted to explore this as I suspect it is one of the most common leaks in poker today. 

These are the 60bb ranges for BTN opens, SB 3-bets, and BTN defends for both range matchups. As in the previous analysis, we will keep one of the ranges unchanged so we can be sure the changes in strategy are driven by the range we’re interested in. BTN is constant, SB is variable.

The GTO range is well-rounded, covering lots of boards. It’s also well-balanced, having a sufficient amount of bluffs of varying strength. Something interesting to note is that having board coverage implies having a certain degree of balance, since selecting hands with lower cards in them also means they’ll be weaker hands. To simulate a more common 3-bet range from the SB, I have given them a super tight range of 99+, AQo+, AJs+, and KQs. Notice how a range like this only has cards with rank 9 or higher, so it can not possibly cover boards where ranks 8 or lower are important. 

Comparing Performance

Once again, let’s look at what the cost of this is, globally, across the 1755 flops. These are the EVs/Equities/EQRs for the first node:

Every metric is elevated for the SB, and the difference in EV is massive. They make an extra 3.48bb on average, which is huge. That sounds great for the SB, so let’s look at the strategy that generates this gain.

SB’s First Action

The SB went from checking 38.6% of the time with their GTO range to just checking 6.7% when their range is overly strong because it lacked preflop bluffs. Meaning, they practically almost always range bet across the 1755 flops. 

Those extra bets mostly go into the 69% pot bet sizing, so not only does the SB bet more often, but they do so for a larger size more often. My initial read on this is that, like in the last example, equity denial is so much more important. The SB more often has a strong one pair hand, but less often has straights, straight draws, flushes, or flush draws, so they need to set a worse price for their opponent’s draws. 

BTN Response to SB’s Most Common (40% Pot) C-Bet Size

The BTN folds way more often, almost twice as often in fact. They also raise less often. 

The SB range is so strong that the BTN has to fold the flop more (a quick reminder, in a perfect world, the BTN would have changed their preflop range in response to such a strong range anyway), and they have to adopt a passive bluff catching strategy when they don’t. 

Why don’t we all just play like Nits?

So when the SB has a super tight range, they get to bet all the time, they capture more EV, and their opponent has to fold more often. 

Why exactly is it a bad strategy to play such a tight 3-betting range? 

I scratched my head about this and eventually got my answer by looking at the one metric that goes down for the SB: equity realization. 

It was higher at the start of the hand in No Bluffs World, but these are the global numbers when the SB bets:

In no-bluffs world, the SB makes less in EV despite having higher equity, and at the same time, their EQR decreases. I’ll spare you going through every node, but this happens with most decision points across these 1755 hands. The no-bluffs range does not realize equity as well as the GTO range. 

Going back to the last decision point we looked at, the BTN folded 25.8% of the time in GTO World compared to 44.4% of the time in No Bluffs World. That’s exactly the problem with overly tight strategies; the big hands get paid off much less often compared to when there is the threat of getting bluffed. 

Players who play like this, which includes myself at times, get positive reinforcement with this strategy because they win the pot often when they do it. But they don’t win a huge pot very often, nor do they benefit from their tight image with bluffs. 

That is the problem with this type of capped range: it is a huge opportunity cost. 

I ran this by my coach, Dara O’Kearney, and he suggested that I look at the EV of AA on a random flop to see this demonstrated in detail. In both scenarios, I put up a Q♥T♥2♦ flop. This is what AA makes:

Every combination of AA makes less in the no-bluffs scenario because it does not get called often enough. 

When the No-Bluffs Guy Doesn’t 3-Bet

There’s another problem the same player will run into; they’ll have to play a range that’s too wide when they don’t 3-bet preflop (i.e., they just flat the BTN’s open). I ran a report for this, too, where I put all the GTO bluffs that I pulled out of the 3-betting range back into the flatting range. 

I won’t go into detail here, but a quick look at the EVs:

In no-bluffs world, the SB loses 0.05bb on average because their range is too wide now. You won’t see much difference in the overall strategy, but it is a leak. And an important reminder that sometimes the biggest leaks come from branches of the game tree you wouldn’t think to look at first.

Conclusion

Capping your range by not having board coverage obviously leaves you vulnerable on low-connected boards, but we have seen that it also hurts your EV overall. The custom aggregated reports have shown us that the broad exploit against these players is to both lead and check-raise more frequently.

When you cap your range like this, it seems great at first glance. We can always bet, and our opponent will fold often. The problem with this is the perennial problem the nit faces: not getting paid. Over-folding is bad for us when we have strong hands, and we don’t get to realize our equity anywhere near as much as we want. 

These are just two experiments I was able to run with custom aggregated reports. They are proving to be an excellent tool for forming a picture of the broad strategic adjustments, which then paves the way for understanding the universally applicable mechanisms that drive those adjustments. This sort of preparation will help you to digest the details of the 1755 individual flops more easily.

item.title: Responding to 3-bets in Straddle+Ante Games
item.description: Previously, we explored opening and 3-betting in Straddle+Ante games. In this article, we wrap up the topic by examining how to respond to 3-bets.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Brokos
item.content:encoded:
Straddle+Ante Hold'em games incentivize players to contest the pot with wider ranges than they would in traditional Hold'em. They also complicate decisions around raise sizing, forcing players to choose between offering a worse price to the player most likely to contest the pot with them and minimizing their exposure to other players who have not yet acted.

As a late position raiser, you should attack these inflated preflop pots aggressively. You should also be prepared for aggressive pushback from the Blinds and Straddle.

In this article, we’ll examine BTN’s response to 3-bets from each OOP opponent to see how position, raise size, and stack depth influence their range construction.

Raise Sizing

Even more so than in two-blind Hold‘em, your response to re-steals should depend heavily on the size of your initial raise, the size of the 3-bet, and the size of the remaining stacks.

There is not necessarily a single “correct” opening size, especially when it comes to opening from the BTN. We offer sims for 4x, 5x, 6x, and 7x opening strategies, and each has its pluses and minuses. Most importantly:

  • Smaller raises benefit the Straddle (STR) at the expense of the Blinds. The STR can profitably call more hands to a small raise, while the Blinds must consider not only their immediate pot odds but also the risk of other players calling or squeezing behind them. They should still continue wider to a smaller raise, but not proportionately wider.
  • Conversely, larger raises benefit the Blinds at the expense of the STR. Larger steals cause the Blinds to win more when they wake up with strong hands, and their weaker hands often would not have been able to call even if faced with a smaller raise. The STR, however, misses out on many calls that would otherwise have been profitable when the BTN opens for a larger size.

More important than the opening size you choose is that you tailor your opening range and your response to 3-bets appropriately. 

When opening for a smaller size, you should have a wider opening range and expect to face smaller (in absolute terms) 3-bets. This means you can anticipate playing postflop with a slightly higher SPR, which will incentivize you to continue with a wider range than you would have had you faced a larger 3-bet after opening for a larger size.

For example, let’s compare two scenarios. In the first, BTN opens for a min-raise (4bb), and SB 3-bets to 20bb. In the second, BTN opens 7bb and SB 3-bets to 24.5bb. In which scenario do you expect BTN to have a higher calling frequency, and why?

Comparison of BTN’s Responses vs. SB 3-Bets

BTN actually calls a good deal more often after opening larger themselves and then facing a larger raise! There are a few reasons for this:

  1. Better odds – This is the most important factor. SB’s 3-bet is larger when facing a larger BTN open but not proportionately larger. This means BTN is getting better odds facing the larger raise in the second scenario. BTN needs to realize 31.3% equity to call in the second scenario but 34% in the first.
  2. Less 4-betting – The larger SB’s 3-bet, the less incentive to 4-bet for the BTN. 4-betting light puts more at risk, and their strongest hands have less incentive to grow the pot when it is already going to be large. So, some hands BTN 4-bets in the first scenario become calls in the second. This includes very strong hands like AA and KK, which provide cover for also calling some weaker hands than they would in the first scenario, such as 22 and 86s.
  3. Tighter opening range – The BTN needs a stronger hand to open 7bb than to open 4bb. Of course, they should also defend more hands when they open wider, but because they are not the only player remaining to act after SB’s 3-bet, they do not defend a proportionate amount of their opening range. Because of the risk posed by BB and STR, SB’s 3-bet must be relatively strong, even if they know BTN will fold disproportionately many weak hands.

It is important to understand these factors because, in real-life game situations, your opponents may not use the same raise sizes as the sims. Nor is this necessarily a mistake on their part. Just as with BTN’s opening size, SB’s choice of 3-bet size (within a reasonable margin) is less about claiming EV for themselves than about how EV is distributed among the remaining players. Smaller 3-bets offer better calling odds to the BTN but lose less when the BB or STR wake up with strong hands. Larger 3-bets take the pot down preflop more often but lose more when the BB or STR wake up with strong hands.

Over the felt, you’ll need to assess the size of the 3-bet you face and be aware of your opening range when constructing your response.

Responding to Re-Steals From Other Positions

Part of the reason why BTN folds disproportionately many of their weakest hands after attempting a small steal is that a SB 3-bet is an unfortunate occurrence. Relative to any other action BTN could face (calls from OOP players, or even raises from players in other positions) a SB 3-bet is the strongest and scariest. 

It is fine and correct to cut your losses with many of your weakest hands when the worst case scenario happens.

As the position of the 3-bettor improves, the gap between BTN’s calling frequencies in the 4bb and 7bb opening scenarios decreases. This is true even though all the other factors incentivizing BTN to call more often in the 7x scenarios are present. 

In fact, BTN calls slightly more often in the 4bb scenario vs. STR, relative to the 7bb scenario. Why do you think this is?

Comparison of BTN’s Responses vs. BB 3-Bets

Comparison of BTN’s Responses vs. STR 3-Bets

Unlike the other seats, the STR in these sims actually does make a proportionately larger 3-bet when facing a larger open. This means BTN is getting better calling odds in the 4bb scenario than in the 7bb scenario, and they will also get to play with a higher SPR after the flop, which favors the in-position (IP) player.

You might also have noticed that BB uses larger 3-bets than SB in these sims and that STR’s 3-bets are still larger. This is a common occurrence in poker: the fewer players there are behind, the larger bets and raises tend to be. The difference is more dramatic when facing a 7bb open than when facing a 4bb open, which is why STR’s 3-bets vs the 7bb open actually offer worse calling odds than their 3-bets vs the 4bb open.

A larger bet size usually indicates a more polar range, and that’s exactly what’s going on here. With more money in the pot and fewer players remaining to act behind them, BB has more incentive to call BTN’s raise than SB does, and STR has even more incentive to call than BB. That means when these players do 3-bet, their ranges should be more polar because they mostly prefer to call the middle of their continuing ranges.

Returning Fire by 4-Betting

BTN has the option to jam or to 4-bet small when facing a 3-bet, and both are an important part of their strategy in our sims. Naturally, they jam more often when facing larger 3-bet, because there is more money in the pot. But even after opening to 4bb and facing a 20bb SB 3-bet (the smallest of the 3-bets in any of these scenarios), BTN has a few jams.

These jams are the usual suspects: AKo, JJ, TT, and some suited wheel Ace-x. All of these hands have poor postflop equity realization, but at the same time solid equity when called after 4-bet shoving. 

The wheel Ace-x have the worst equity when called, but they also have the best blocking effects (in addition to blocking calls, they unblock folds) and the most to gain from fold equity. Stronger pocket pairs gain less from preflop fold equity and have better postflop equity realization, especially when the SPR is low, so they prefer small 4-bets to shoves.BTN’s small 4-betting range is more polar, containing very strong hands that want to induce further action and very weak hands that don’t give up much when they fold to a shove. 

Medium hands that would have tougher or more painful decisions when jammed on prefer either to jam themselves or to call and play after the flop.

These patterns persist in the other scenarios, but because the 3-bets are larger, more hands make their way into the jamming ranges. Specifically, two new types of hand jam in the 7x scenarios but not in the 4x scenarios: small pairs and suited Broadways.

As discussed above, the larger pots incentivize more jamming from BTN, but they also incentivize more calling of those jams from the 3-bettor. The suited Broadways and smaller pairs make their way into these jamming ranges because they have better equity against these wider calling ranges than they would against tight ones. In the case of the small pairs, they also make better jams than medium pairs because they unblock folds and play less well as calls.

Once again, the important skill here is not to memorize these sims but to understand the reasons why the ranges are constructed the way they are. Your opponents, for reasons that may or not be strategically sound, may use different 3-betting strategies than the ones shown in these sims. 

Improvising a sound response on the fly will require understanding your incentives and how they influence your range construction.

Deeper Stacks

Speaking of opponents not using the same raise sizes as the sims, check out SB’s 3-bet size in this 600bb sim:

They’re raising to 40bb, and that’s still not enough to deter BTN from calling with pretty much all their pairs, suited connectors, suited Broadways, and suited Ace-x!

With such deep starting stacks, the SPR when BTN calls the 3-bet will be around 7 despite the enormous raise size. Consequently, BTN’s calling range is oriented towards making straights, flushes, and sets. Of course, these hands will more often make one pair, and that will sometimes be enough to win if the pot doesn’t get too large, but it’s plain to see how much they value the potential to make something stronger.

Aces, Kings, and Ace-King 4-bet not only because they are strong but because most of their strength lies in making one pair. In the 200bb sims from earlier, BTN often flats AA to a 3-bet. That’s because the postflop SPR will be low enough to comfortably stack off with one good pair in a 3-bet pot. When stacks are deeper, Aces needs to 4-bet to get that SPR down to where an overpair will be worth the rest of their chips on most flops.

BB’s 3-bet size is even larger, and BTN’s response is similar, just a bit tighter than it was versus SB:

STR’s size is larger still, and because their 3-betting range is the most polar of the three, BTN is a bit more conservative with their 4-bets:

Adapting to Smaller Raises

Should you encounter smaller 3-bets in deep-stacked scenarios—and you probably will—what does all this tell us about how to respond to them?

You should be ruthless about calling with suited and connected hands, especially when the cards are large. 

Here’s BTN’s response when they open 4bb and face a 20bb 3-bet from SB:

With so much money remaining to wager after the flop, BTN’s superior position is enormously valuable. This subsidizes calls with not just suited Ace-x and suited connectors but most suited King-x and suited gappers. Had you used a larger open raise size and faced a similarly small 3-bet, you should call wider still.

4-betting a less polar range that includes some suited connectors is viable against a smaller raise, as it will be a lot riskier for SB to deny your equity by jamming over your 4-bet. Big pairs and offsuit Broadways remain the very best 4-bet candidates, though.

Conclusion

Straddle+Ante games present players with complex, often competing incentives. Most people playing them have more experience in traditional, two-blind games, and that may (mis)lead them to pursue suboptimal range construction and/or bet sizes. So, you should expect to encounter a variety of re-stealing strategies in these games, and you won’t be able to memorize responses to all of them.

Instead, focus on understanding the principles that should guide your response: position, pot odds, polarity, and stack depth:

  • The worse an opponent’s position, the stronger their 3-betting range, and the tighter your response to that 3-bet.
  • Smaller multiples of your opening size offer better calling odds, even if the raise is large in absolute terms.
  • Larger raises and raises from later positions are more polar, incentivizing more calling and less 4-betting.
  • Playing with deeper stacks favors the IP player after the flop, incentivizing more calls. They can also incentivize more 4-bets as long as they don’t make a 5-bet jam too enticing. Your calls should mostly come from hands with the potential to make straights, flushes, and sets.

Put your newfound knowledge into practice with this drill, which will present you with tough decisions based on the scenarios in this article and some new ones as well!

item.title: Stealing and Restealing in Straddle+Ante Games
item.description:
Most players treat straddle games like a regular game with higher stakes. They're not.
It's a chain reaction that starts preflop and reshapes the entire hand. If you're playing straddle games the same as regular games, you're leaving a lot on the table.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Brokos
item.content:encoded:
Late position openers in Straddle+Ante games face different risks and rewards than they do in traditional two-blind Hold'em. The larger preflop pot creates a stronger incentive to steal, but the additional player behind the Button (who could call or, worse, 3-bet) makes opening riskier.

The players behind the Button also face different incentives when responding to a steal. The antes and the Button's wider opening range increase the value of both calling and 3-betting. At the same time, the larger pot gives the opener greater incentive to call a 3-bet, which in turn affects the hands the Blinds and Straddle choose to 3-bet and the sizings they use. 

We’ll begin by unpacking BTN’s incentives when attempting a steal and when responding to a re-steal. This will provide important context for understanding why the Blinds and Straddle construct their 3-betting ranges the way they do.

The Incentive To Steal

Despite the increased risk of a re-raise, BTN opens a wider range when there are antes in the pot. Stealing the antes is obviously the optimal outcome for those loose opens, but if someone calls the raise, BTN will still do well postflop when playing in position (IP). Even when faced with a 3-bet, which is generally the worst outcome, many mediocre hands will be able to defend thanks to pot odds provided by the antes.

BTN Steal

BTN opens 47.1% of hands for 7bb (3.5str) in an unraked Straddle+Ante game, compared to 40.5% for a 3bb raise in an unraked two-blind game. The composition of the ranges is similar; the antes simply incentivize BTN to open slightly weaker versions of the same hands they would in a traditional structure.

BTN Response vs Re-Steal (From the Last Actor)

Faced with a 3-bet from the BB in a two-blind game, BTN continues by calling with 36.6% of their opening range. In contrast, when facing a 3-bet from the STR in a Straddle+Ante game, BTN calls with as much as 53.1% of it. Despite this difference, 4-betting frequencies remain similar in both scenarios.

Players responding to a steal in a Straddle+Ante game can expect a wider stealing range but also a more stubborn (call-heavy) response to a re-steal. 

Let’s see how those competing incentives affect each player’s range construction.

SB Facing BTN Open

Traditional two-blind Hold‘em offers the SB little incentive to call a steal. Even in an unraked game, they respond mostly by raising or folding.

Antes, however, fundamentally change this dynamic. SB still responds quite tightly to a BTN open, as their position is terrible, but they actually call more than they raise:

We can broadly describe their ranges as follows:

  • Raise: Best pocket pairs, best offsuit Broadways, lower suited Broadways, and lower suited Aces
  • Call: Lower pocket pairs, best suited Broadways, best suited Aces, lower offsuit Broadways with straight potential

Preflop hand selection is essentially choosing which tools to bring to a job. 

SB Re-Steal

When SB 3-bets, they will often end up playing heads up after the flop with a relatively low SPR. Big pocket pairs and offsuit Broadways are the best tools for this kind of job, because they flop strong pairs relatively easily. And that’s generally all you need to stack off when heads up with a low SPR.

SB Call

SB’s calls, on the other hand, are geared toward playing with a higher SPR and/or multiple opponents. Their calling range includes many combos that are often described as “speculative.” They don’t make strong hands as often as the big pairs and Broadway cards, but when they do, they make stronger hands like sets, straights, and flushes, which can put more money into the pot against more opponents. Just what the job calls for.

BB Facing BTN Open

BB’s response is not terribly different from SB’s. In fact, their 3-betting strategy is nearly identical. The major difference is that, getting a better price and with only one player remaining to act behind them, they can call with weaker speculative hands. BB’s calling range includes suited connectors, suited gappers, and suited Kings and Queens, which SB’s does not. It also includes some weaker offsuit Aces, which nevertheless dominate a substantial portion of BTN’s opening range.

STR Facing BTN Open

STR responds a bit differently than the Blinds. In particular, they 3-bet more of their best hands, such as bigger pocket pairs and suited Broadways. With no one to act behind them, they will never induce a squeeze or contest a pot multiway after calling. That makes their calling range more obviously capped than those of the Blinds. 

The diversity of STR’s calling range ensures they will make strong hands on virtually all flops, even if they never carry forward any strong preflop hands in their calling range.

The large preflop pot and the small number of players remaining to act also put a new option on the table for STR: jamming all-in. This isn’t much used at equilibrium, but unlike in two-blind Hold‘em, it’s an option worth considering in real-life game situations. The hands that jam are mostly AKo, JTs, and 99, hands with good raw equity but poor postflop equity realization. These jams win 14.5bb when BTN folds, and they aren’t in terrible shape against BTN’s calling range. Other jams, like A2o and K9o, perform less well when called but block BTN’s calling range while unblocking their folding range.

Continuation Betting

We’ll need to approach this topic with a grain of salt because the only aggregate reports available for two-blind Hold‘em cash games are for raked games, while the Straddle+Ante reports do not include rake. Even so, the differences between the two are dramatic enough to draw some larger conclusions about how postflop play differs in Straddle+Ante games as a result of the different preflop incentives.

Here’s BB’s aggregate c-betting strategy for a raked, 9-handed 100bb cash game with a 2.5bb open from the BTN:

BB checks a little more than half their range on average after their 3-bet (to 13bb) is called. When they do bet, they mostly bet 50% or 75% pot, suggesting a more polarized strategy.

BB’s worst flops are heavy on medium cards and mostly monotone. On these flops, they do not c-bet at all.

Compare this to a STR vs BTN 3-bet pot (unraked, with a 3.5str opening size and a 14str 3-bet size):

STR checks less than a quarter of their range, and 33% pot is their most used size. This suggests a more linear c-betting strategy and a bigger equity advantage, which makes sense. Whereas BB in a two-blind game favors a polar 3-betting strategy, STR expects BTN to call more often because of the antes, and so 3-bets a more linear, equity-dense range. This, along with BTN’s wider calling range, means STR flops more equity on average and so bets more often. The small bets, in particular, target BTN’s total whiffs, of which they will have more when they call with more weak hands preflop.

The worst flops for c-betting are still mostly monotone, but for the STR, they are more often high and disconnected. BTN’s expanded calling range includes a lot more offsuit Broadway hands, which increases the risk that a light c-bet will be drawing nearly dead to top pair on these flops.  

We see a similar pattern when we compare SB vs BTN c-betting in a two-blind game to BB vs BTN c-betting in a straddle+ante game:

Conclusion

Antes change everything. By incentivizing a wider stealing range and a more stubborn response to re-steals, they also incentivize a more linear, equity-dense 3-betting range from the defending players. This, in turn, incentivizes more and smaller flop c-bets to capitalize on the 3-bettor’s equity advantage.

For a deeper look at how to respond to these 3-bets, see our guide to responding to 3-bets in Straddle+Ante games.

Ready to practice your new skills? This drill throws you into the action as either SB, BB, or STR facing a BTN steal.

Why Late-Stage Decisions Matter

Most MTT regs study chip EV strategies which are designed to accumulate chips rather than maximize $EV. In a previous exploration, we showed that chip EV strategies lose a significant amount of money in late stages, especially near the bubble and final table.

But why does that matter if late-stage tournament spots are less common?

As Andrew Brokos explains in Tournament Poker's Hidden Stakes, your buy-in tells you what's at stake at the start, but that can grow enormously as you progress. By the final table, a single decision can involve tournament equity worth many times your original investment. That's why late-stage skill can have such an outsized impact on your results. You reach those spots less often, but once you do, o decision can be worth more than a month of regular grinding.

2026 Main Event Example

Picture this. You're a midstack on the biggest final table of your life. The short-stacked HJ opens 2bb, the BTN raises almost all of their chips, effectively all-in. You look down at pocket Jacks in the BB.

What's your play?

That was Greg Mueller's decision at the 2026 WSOP Main Event, with $2.25 million already locked and $10 million up top.

Han Feng, the shortest stack, min-opens HJ with A♦A♣. In chip EV that's just an open-jam at 8bb. Under ICM, aces prefer the small raise, splitting off from the rest of the range.

Saaskilahti 3-bets 9♠9♥, leaving about 3bb behind. That "almost all in" sizing is a real ICM tactic: it keeps a fold available if a covering stack jams behind him. The problem is his hand. Feng's min-open has already polarized his range, so in theory 99 is too thin to 3-bet.

Then it's on Mueller in BB with Jacks. He's got 22bb and $2.25 million already in his pocket. Tough spot.

He tank-folds. PokerNews called it a brilliant fold. Let's check.

According to GTO, folding is the correct play, although it’s right on the cusp. Pocket jacks sit at the very edge of a narrow optimal shoving range, so both shoving and folding are viable options.

Here's the part worth thinking about. How much tighter should you play in this spot with ICM pressure?

How much does the payout pressure affect this decision? In chip EV, jacks facing a min-open and a short 3-bet are a snap jam, the kind of decision that's so easy you have to remind yourself to fake hesitation. ICM took a rather easy spot and made it hard. Mueller was right to recognize that it was a close decision.

And then, in a twist of fate, Feng called all in for his 25M, and the nines made a straight on the river to crack the aces.

Lock in your Early Bird rate now: an annual Ultra plan locked before October 15 is the cheapest Ultra will ever be.

Preflop ICM Solving requires Ultra on the Tournament plan. Anyone can try preflop solving (including ICM & Rake) for free up to 10bb effective.

3-Way Postflop ICM Solving

Once your preflop spot is solved, GTO Wizard AI carries the ranges, stacks, and payouts straight into postflop, so the flop strategy you study is built on the exact preflop ranges you just solved.

A chip leader, a middle stack, and a short stack see a flop. The same bet puts each player under a different kind of pressure. Now you can solve the whole interaction with ICM and bounties built in.

A middle stack can face a difficult decision when losing the pot means busting before a shorter stack. A valuable bounty can make fighting for that same pot more attractive. And the player behind you can change which bets, calls, and raises are profitable before they've even acted. Understanding those competing incentives is a huge opportunity to separate yourself from players relying on chip EV intuition.

Now you can test the details that decide these pots. Compare the same flop under ICM and chip EV. Change who covers whom. Increase a bounty. Nodelock an opponent who calls too loosely and see how both remaining players should adjust. Each comparison helps you understand which part of the tournament setup is driving the strategy.

  • Ultra builds fully custom 3-way ICM solutions: your own bet sizes, ranges, stacks, payouts, bounties, nodelocks, and Player Profiles.
  • Elite browses ready-made 3-way ICM Single Size solutions in Study and Practice. This is the same split that already applies to our chip EV 3-way solutions.

Why Fold EV Isn't Always Zero

In a simple chip EV spot, if you fold, you win no chips, so we measure the value of other decisions relative to that option. But tournament utility is measured in tournament equity (ICM value), not chips. Survival is what matters.

When you fold in a multiway spot, it can change the strategies of the players behind you, which in turn affects your tournament equity. Those players can clash, knock each other out, or make mistakes that leak tournament equity to you. You can ladder without winning another chip. For example, say you are 1 of 3 players remaining, but the last 2 are maniacs in the blinds. You might be more willing to fold on the BTN to let them clash. Setting fold EV to 0 would hide that information.

On a more cerebral point, folding generates a card removal effect that can theoretically alter optimal strategy among the remaining active players, which in turn affects your tournament equity. This means that some hands actually generate more EV than others when folding, and again, setting that to some flat number like 0 is misleading.
